name: Little Venice
label: Little Venice
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Little Venice' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5522991921 (Little Venice): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront houses with colourful balconies hanging over the sea, best at sunset.

text.description: Little Venice is a row of 18th-century captains' houses whose balconies hang out over the water, with the Aegean right behind them. That mix of old houses, sea and open sky is why it is so popular with visitors, and guides call it the most photographed viewpoint on the island. The best-known angle is from the small promenade at the north end, looking south along the balconies. From there you get clean, front-on shots of the building facades without too much clutter in the frame. A phone copes well here, because the whole scene is close and colourful. Stand still for a moment before you shoot and check that the horizon and the balcony lines are straight. If you have time, try a second shot a little lower or from a different corner so that the water fills more of the picture. The place gets very crowded from late afternoon in summer, and the terrace seats fill up before sunset, so arrive early if you want a clear view. Two nearby spots give a different take. Kato Mili shows the whitewashed windmills in the foreground with Little Venice and the bay below, but it is often windy at the top. Panagia Paraportiani gives a lower angle of Little Venice with the windmills in the background; take care on the uneven ground there.
text.geographic_location: Little Venice is on the Mykonos waterfront. It sits close to the Kato Mili windmills and the Panagia Paraportiani church.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for the island, so make your way directly to Little Venice on the Mykonos waterfront. It is the row of houses with balconies right over the sea. For the best-known view, go to the small promenade at the north end of the row. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole row of balconies and the sea into one frame from the small promenade. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out balcony and window details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you see the row of 18th-century captains' houses with their balconies over the water, framed against the Aegean.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the balcony row with one of the horizontal lines so the houses do not lean. Keep a strip of sea or sky in the frame to show how close the houses are to the water. For a different view, try Kato Mili for the windmills in the foreground with Little Venice below, or Panagia Paraportiani for a lower angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the whitewashed walls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white does not wash out and the sea and sky keep their colour. If the light is low near sunset, hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Take a few frames in case someone walks through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 45 minutes before sunset, before the promenade fills with people. Some visitors prefer sunrise for emptier streets.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public place and the view itself does not need a ticket; terrace seats are separate and fill up before sunset.

name: Mykonos windmills
label: Kato Mili windmills
camera_source: Commons cluster (82 photos). Moved 16 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/299878763: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Windmills' (112 m across).
notes: The iconic row of white windmills above the sea at the edge of Mykonos Town.

text.description:
The Mykonos windmills are the island's best-known skyline: a row of round, whitewashed towers with pointed roofs and very small windows, standing on a hill above the town and the sea. There are 16 windmills on the island, and seven of them stand on this hill in Chora, the main town. Most were built by the Venetians in the 16th century, though building carried on into the early 20th century. They ground wheat and were an important source of income for local people until production stopped in the middle of the 20th century. One of them is now a museum.

They photograph well because the shapes are simple and repeat: white walls, pointed roofs and a lot of open sky. Most of them face north, towards the strongest winds. Take one wide shot to show the whole row against the sky, then step closer for a single tower with its door and small windows. Look down the hill too: Chora and part of the harbour can be seen from this high ground, and they make a good second picture with the windmills at the edge of the frame. Allow a few minutes, as other visitors will be walking through your shot.
text.geographic_location: On the hill overlooking the harbour on the edge of Chora (Mykonos Town), on the island of Mykonos in the Cyclades.
text.directions_text: Start from Mykonos Town (Chora), the island's main village; the windmills can be seen from almost anywhere in it. If you are coming from elsewhere on the island, get to Chora (Mykonos Town) first. From the phone icon on the map it is about 1 minute on foot to the windmills, which lie to the south-west. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole row against the sky, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out one windmill or the town below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take your wide shots from here, then walk the minute or so towards them for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the row of windmills along the lower third, leaving the sky above. Keep the horizon level, as the white towers make any tilt obvious. For a close shot, frame one windmill with its pointed roof against clear sky and keep other visitors out of the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white does not turn grey or lose detail in bright sun. If the sky looks flat, tap on it and check the brightness again.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower, gives softer light and more shape to the white walls. Early or late in the day is often calmer too, but check on the day.

text.access_note: The windmills are on a hill in the town, but one of them is a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Paradise Beach
label: Paradise Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Paradise Beach' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W366448872 (Paradise Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous sandy beach on the south coast, known for its beach clubs.

text.description:
Paradise Beach is a beach on Mykonos, and it photographs well because of its shape. The sand curves around a bay, with beach clubs, umbrellas and sunbeds lined up along it. That repeating pattern gives a phone photo plenty of colour and structure.

The best overview comes from the rocks at the edges of the bay, above the beach clubs. From up there you can see the whole bay at once, with the umbrellas and sunbeds running along the sand. A guide also says these rocks work well for a photoshoot, so they suit portraits of friends with the bay behind them. Check on the day that the rocks are still accessible.

On the sand, look for simple compositions: the water's edge, rows of sunbeds, or one umbrella against the sea. Early morning is suggested for quieter water and sand compositions. In high season, expect crowds and music from the beach clubs, so keep people out of the frame or use them to show the atmosphere. Try a wide shot first, then a closer one of a detail such as a row of umbrellas. Keep your phone lens clean, as sea air and sunscreen quickly smear it.
text.geographic_location: Paradise Beach is on the coast of Mykonos, on a bay lined with beach clubs. Agia Anna is a separate beach nearby.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stop is listed for this spot. The viewpoint is the rocks at the edges of the bay, above the beach clubs, and the phone icon on the map is on Paradise Beach. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the rocks to fit the whole bay and the line of beach clubs into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the umbrellas and sunbeds. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a row of umbrellas or a single detail on the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Paradise Beach, on the rocks at the edges of the bay, above the beach clubs. From here the photo shows a wide view of the whole bay, with the beach clubs and their umbrellas and sunbeds lining the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on one of the lines so the bay looks level. Let the curve of the sand lead the eye along the picture. For a portrait, use portrait mode with your subject on the rocks and the bay behind. Panorama also works if you move slowly and keep the phone steady. Wait for people to move out of the way before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the beach clubs or your subject, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so the pale sand and sky keep their detail. Clean the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is suggested for quieter water and sand compositions, and it also means fewer people and less music.

text.access_note: Check on the day that the rocks are still accessible.

name: Psarou
label: Psarou Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Psarou Beach' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/366448875: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Psarou' (265 m across).
notes: Glamorous sandy bay on the south coast.

text.description: Psarou is a sandy beach and small village on the island of Mykonos, set around a sheltered bay. It photographs well because the scene is so simple: a curve of sand, clear water and large yachts anchored offshore. The sea gives you a clean, bright backdrop, and the boats add scale and something to build the shot around. The beach is about 4 km from Mykonos town (Chora) and close to Platys Gialos. The village had a population of 106 as of 2021, so it is a small place. For the best pictures, walk onto the public sand facing the bay, away from the beach club loungers, so that sunbeds and umbrellas do not crowd the foreground. From there you can include the water, the sand and the yachts in one frame. Late afternoon is a good time to come, when the light on the bay is warm and the yachts show up as dark shapes against the sea. If you prefer a calmer picture of the bay, go early in the morning, before the loungers fill the front of the beach from late morning. A higher viewpoint above the beach may give a downward view over the beach and bay, but check the map first. Keep your phone's gridlines on to hold the horizon level.
text.geographic_location: Psarou is on the island of Mykonos, about 4 km from Mykonos town (Chora) and close to Platys Gialos.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops serve this spot, so start from Mykonos town (Chora), about 4 km away, and check your route on the map. Once at Psarou Beach, walk onto the public sand facing the bay and stand away from the beach club loungers. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bay, sand and yachts together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sea and sky, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single yacht.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the beach and the bay are right in front of you, and the anchored yachts sit out on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep a strip of clean sand at the bottom of the frame and let the yachts sit on the water line. For a different view, check the map for a higher viewpoint above the beach that may give a downward look over the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or the yachts to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and white sand do not wash out. At low light, night mode can help, but hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is golden and the yachts make good silhouettes. Early morning is quieter, before the beach club sets up.

text.access_note: The beach itself is public sand, but the beach club area is paid, so shoot from the public sand and check the official site before you go if you plan to use any club facilities.

name: Church of Panagia Paraportiani
label: Paraportiani Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Panagia Paraportiani' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/623949364: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Panagia Paraportiani' (26 m across).
notes: Whitewashed church of five joined chapels, the most photographed building on the island.

text.description: The Church of Panagia Paraportiani is a striking whitewashed church in Chora (Mykonos Town), and it is easy to see why people photograph it. Its whitewashed walls are lumpy and layered rather than neat, so the whole church looks almost sculpted against the sky. It is really five churches joined together: four sit at ground level and form the base of a fifth built on top. Work began in 1425 and was not finished until the 17th century. The name means "Our Lady of the Side Gate", because the entrance was once by the side gate into the Kastro area. For a phone photo, the usual choice is the front view from the square, which fills the frame with white curves and sky. When that is busy, walk down and to the left of the church to the rocky outcrop on the seaward side. From there you get a lower angle with open sea behind the church. From the rocks below you can look across Little Venice towards the windmills in the distance. If you want a wider, higher view, the hillside above Little Venice (known as Alefkandra) shows the church against the sea and the white houses around it. Take your time on the rocks, as the footing can be uneven.
text.geographic_location: The church stands in the Kastro neighbourhood of Chora (Mykonos Town), on the seaward edge of the old town, close to Little Venice.
text.directions_text: Head for Chora (Mykonos Town), then continue on foot into the Kastro neighbourhood, where the church stands. Little Venice is nearby. The subject is the church itself; for the seaward angle, walk down and to the left of the church to the rocky outcrop. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the church with the sea behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the rocks to take in Little Venice and the windmills, and try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the windmills in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the seaward angle, walk down and to the left of the church to the rocky outcrop on the seaward side, which is a nearby alternative viewpoint. From there you get a lower angle of the church with open sea behind it. From the rocks below you can look across Little Venice with the windmills in the distance. Take care climbing down onto the rocks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the church's white mass on one side of the frame, with the sea filling the rest. Keep the horizon level. If the square in front of the church is crowded, this seaward angle is a good alternative. For a wider, higher view of the church against the sea and the white houses, try the hillside above Little Venice (Alefkandra).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the whitewash keeps its texture and the sky stays blue. Take a few frames, as sea spray and passers-by can spoil a single shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: As general advice only, early morning or late afternoon often gives softer light on white walls than midday.

text.access_note: The outside of the church can be visited freely, but the inside opens only at service times, so check locally before you go.

name: Ftelia
label: Ftelia Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ftelia Archeological Site' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1472325: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wide windswept beach on the north coast, popular with windsurfers.

text.description:
Ftelia is a beach on the north side of Mykonos, and it is also the site of a very old village. People lived here around 5000 to 4500 BC, in the Late Neolithic. Diggers found wall foundations, pottery, stone tools, traces of early metalworking and 19 small stone figurines. One find is a circular gold object, thought to be the earliest securely dated gold from the Aegean. The village is thought to have housed roughly 150 to 200 people.

For a photo, the appeal is the mix of history and open scenery. Low stone walls sit on a small rise above the middle of the beach, and the sand, the sea and the wide bay stretch out behind them. It feels quieter and more unusual than the usual beach shot. Keep your expectations modest: the walls are low and some finds are no longer visible, so treat them as a foreground detail rather than the main attraction.

The site is still being excavated, so large parts are closed. Stay on the marked paths and do not step into the dig area. The beach is often windy and dusty, which is why it is usually quiet, even in high summer. Wipe your phone lens before shooting, and hold the phone with both hands.
text.geographic_location: Ftelia is on the north coast of Mykonos, on a windswept sandy bay. The ruins sit on the slope just above the centre of the beach.
text.directions_text: There is no public transport to Ftelia, and the last stretch to the beach is a dirt road, so take it slowly. Check how to get there before you go. Once at the beach, walk up to the low ruins on the rise above its centre. The phone icon on the map is right at the site, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walls, beach and bay together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a very low, sweeping foreground, and keep the phone level so the horizon does not bend.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the low prehistoric stone walls fill the foreground, with the sandy beach, the sea and the windswept bay behind them. Stay on the marked paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch a little and put a stretch of wall in the bottom third of the frame, with the beach curving away behind it and the sea along the top. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight. For a wider alternative, Ftelia Beach itself gives a broad view of the sandy bay and sea, with the beach spread out below the bar terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stones to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and sea keep their colour. Use a 2x zoom to pick out a single wall without leaning into the ruins. Wind can shake the phone, so brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Any time of day works. Pick a calmer spell if you can, as the wind and dust can be strong.

text.access_note: The ruins belong to an active excavation, so large parts are closed to the public; stay on marked paths, and check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Wind can shake a handheld phone, so bracing your elbows helps.
Dust can build up on a phone lens, so wiping it before shooting helps.

name: Archaeological Museum of Mykonos
label: Archaeological Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1988490509: the OpenStreetMap point 'Archaeological Museum Of Mykonos'.
notes: Houses finds from Delos and Rheneia, including large painted vases.

text.description:
The Archaeological Museum of Mykonos is located near the Old Port on the island of Mykonos. It is a modest neoclassical building, and it makes a calm, tidy subject for a phone camera. Pale walls, regular windows and a formal entrance give you clean lines, which suit a phone camera well.

The museum was established in 1902 by the Greek Archaeological Service. It was first built to hold finds from a burial site on the nearby islet of Rineia (Rhenia), dating back to 425/426 BC. The original building dates from 1905. It was refurbished and extended in the 1930s and 1960s, and a large eastern room was added in 1972. Inside, the collection includes pottery, funerary urns and sculpture. Its best-known piece is the large Mykonos vase, which shows scenes from the fall of Troy.

For photographs, think of this as an architecture and street-scene stop rather than a sweeping view. Take a straight-on shot of the façade, then step back and include a little of the street so the building feels part of the town. Keep your phone level, using the gridlines, so the vertical lines of the walls stay upright. Photography rules inside the museum can differ, so check the official site before you go, and take your pictures of the exterior from the street.
text.geographic_location: The museum is near the Old Port on the island of Mykonos.
text.directions_text: Mykonos has no Underground, tram or similar stops. Start from the Old Port, near which the museum stands. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the building. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the doorway or window frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the entrance, then step back along whatever space is available if you want to fit in the whole façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the edges of the building up with the vertical lines, so the walls stay straight. Keep a little street or sky around the building so it does not look cramped. Try a second shot at 2x on the entrance and the stonework. If people walk through the frame, wait a moment and shoot again.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch if the white looks too bright. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls. Use the ultra-wide sparingly, as it can stretch the edges of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the street. Midday sun can make the white walls harsh.

text.access_note: Check the museum's official information before you go for visiting arrangements and photography rules; the exterior can be photographed from the street.

name: Aegean Maritime Museum
label: Aegean Maritime Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/736557080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Aegean Maritime Museum' (17 m across).
notes: Small museum of Greek seafaring history in the old town.

text.description: The Aegean Maritime Museum sits in a 19th-century Mykonian building in the Tria Pigadia area of the town centre. The Armenistis Lighthouse, built in 1890, stands in the garden and gives you a strong upright shape to build a picture around. The garden also holds a number of ancient sailors' marble gravestones gathered from Mykonos and Delos, which make good close-up details. The museum is a non-profit institution, founded in 1983 and open to the public since 1985. It focuses on Greek maritime history and especially on the merchant ships of the Aegean. For a phone photo, start at the phone icon on the map and look for the clean lines of the building and any lighthouse or garden view that is visible. Keep the frame simple: one main subject, with a bit of sky or wall around it. If you have little room to step back, a wider lens helps. Be considerate of other visitors, and check opening times locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Tria Pigadia area of Mykonos Town (Chora), in the town centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for Mykonos, so start from Mykonos Town centre. Head for the Tria Pigadia area in the town centre. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the building and garden in tight spaces, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the lighthouse and the carved gravestone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It is at the museum itself, so you are right at the subject. Look around for the best view of the building and garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the lighthouse or the main building on one of the vertical lines to keep it straight. Hold the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a second picture, move in close with the telephoto lens on a gravestone or a stone detail, with the garden softly behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the building or lighthouse, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the walls and sky keep their detail. Try portrait mode on the gravestone details if you want a soft background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and less harsh. Midday sun can wash out the detail.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so check opening times before you go.

name: Panagia Tourliani Monastery
label: Panagia Tourliani
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ano Mera Square' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ano Mera' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM W303099999 (Tourliani Monastery): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: 16th-century monastery with a carved marble bell tower in Ano Mera village.

text.description: Panagia Tourliani is the monastery at the heart of Ano Mera, and its white marble bell tower is the part most visitors photograph. The tower has three bells and several crosses, and from the village square it stands out cleanly against the sky. The square gives you room to step back, so the whole tower fits in one frame without tilting your phone upwards. The monastery is also an active place of worship. Inside the grounds, the whitewashed church facade with its red-shuttered details and the courtyard in front make a second, more intimate picture. The courtyard needs you to go into the monastery grounds, so check the entrance fee and opening hours locally before you go. Whichever view you choose, keep it respectful: don't use flash, don't photograph services, and ask first if you want to take pictures inside the church. For the tower, go in the late afternoon, when low light from the west falls on the marble. Keep an eye on the light, because the tower falls into full shade, so aim to shoot about 30 minutes before that. Turn on your gridlines so the tower's vertical lines stay straight, and leave a little sky above the crosses.
text.geographic_location: In the village of Ano Mera on Mykonos, close to Ano Mera Square.
text.directions_text: The monastery is about 1 minute on foot from it, to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole tower with some sky around it. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the bells and crosses. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the courtyard if you go in, to fit in the church facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ano Mera Square (far corner of the square, facing the bell tower). The monastery's white marble bell tower with its three bells and crosses, framed against the sky from the square. In the far corner of the square, facing the bell tower. From there the white marble tower, with its three bells and crosses, is framed against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the tower up with one of the vertical lines. Leave a little sky above the crosses and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean inwards. If you go into the courtyard, the whitewashed church facade with its red shutters makes a good alternative shot, as long as you are allowed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white marble keeps its detail. Turn the flash off, especially near the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, starting about 30 minutes before the tower falls into full shade.

text.access_note: The square is not a paid viewpoint, but the monastery is an active place of worship, so check the fee and hours before you go, and ask before photographing inside.

name: Agios Stefanos
label: Agios Stefanos Beach

notes: Calm beach north of town with a view back to the island's coast.

text.description: Agios Stefanos is a small whitewashed chapel with a red dome, standing at the far end of Agios Stefanos beach. Its name means Saint Stephen. The beach is a sandy stretch beside Tourlos, the newer harbour of Mykonos. It is busy in summer, with sunbeds, umbrellas, water sports, hotels, restaurants and cafes close by. The chapel is a calm contrast to all that. It works well on a phone because the shapes are simple: bright white walls and a red dome, with the blue bay behind and the island of Delos on the horizon. Stand at the front of the chapel, facing the sea, and you can keep the building in the foreground and let the water and Delos fill the background. The chapel is rarely open to visitors, so plan to photograph it from outside. If you want a second picture, walk onto the beach and frame the chapel and its red roof against the water. Midday sun in summer can wash out the white walls, so early morning or late afternoon gives you more detail. Sunset is the favourite time here, when the light falls over the water towards Delos. Take a few frames at different distances.
text.geographic_location: Next to Tourlos, the new harbour of Mykonos, at the far end of Agios Stefanos beach. It is about 3.5 km from Mykonos town.
text.directions_text: Start in Mykonos town, about 3.5 km away. You can reach the beach by regular bus from Mykonos town, or by taxi or private vehicle. Once on the sand, walk to the far end of the beach, where the chapel stands facing the sea and Delos. Walk or look south from there to the chapel. For the classic view, continue to the front of the chapel and face the sea. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the chapel with the bay and Delos behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the beach and sky. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), try 2x or 3x for a tighter shot of the red dome against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Front of the chapel at the far end of Agios Stefanos beach, facing the sea and the island of Delos). The whitewashed chapel with its red dome in the foreground, with the blue bay and Delos behind it. From here the chapel is a distant subject to the south. For the classic view, walk to the front of the chapel at the far end of Agios Stefanos beach and face the sea, so the whitewashed chapel with its red dome is in the foreground, with the blue bay and Delos behind it. For an alternative, walk onto Agios Stefanos Beach and stand with the sun behind you, so the chapel and its red roof are framed against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the chapel on one third of the frame, leaving the bay and Delos on the other. Keep the phone level so the horizon stays straight. Hold the phone low for a bit more sea and sky, or step back to include the whole building. The beach viewpoint, with the sun behind you, is a good second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white walls keep their detail and don't turn flat. At sunset, check the horizon and Delos before you take the shot, and take a few frames as the light changes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the favourite time for the view towards Delos. Early morning or late afternoon is also good. Avoid roughly 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. in summer, when glare washes out the white walls.

text.access_note: The beach is public and the chapel is a small place of worship that is rarely open to visitors, so photograph it from outside.
claims_not_in_sources: Delos lies across the water in the direction of the sunset, so the sun sets towards it.
The beach can be crowded in summer, so the chapel front may be busy at sunset.
Telephoto lenses at 2x-5x depend on the phone model.
Early morning and late afternoon light is softer than midday light.
